title: How to Convert Your Hourly Rate to Annual Pay: Salary Sacrifice Electric Car and More
description: Learn how to convert hourly to annual pay using a 38-hour week, 52-week year. Includes salary sacrifice electric car, tax, super, and fortnightly pay.
salarySummary: Annual pay is your hourly rate multiplied by 38 hours per week times 52 weeks, assuming a standard full-time week.

faqs.q: How does salary sacrifice electric car affect my annual pay calculation?
faqs.a: Salary sacrificing an electric car reduces your taxable income because the lease payments and running costs are taken from your pre-tax salary. This lowers the gross annual figure used for tax, but your employer still pays super on your ordinary earnings (the amount before the sacrifice). The calculator on this site does not deduct salary sacrifice, so you need to manually subtract the annual sacrifice amount from your gross pay to estimate your taxable income. For example, if you earn $80,000 and sacrifice $10,000 for an electric car, your taxable income becomes $70,000. The tax saving depends on your marginal rate and the fringe benefits tax treatment, which for eligible electric cars is currently exempt under the Australian Taxation Office rules.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my fortnightly pay from an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Fortnightly pay is simply your weekly pay multiplied by two. For a 38-hour week, weekly pay equals your hourly rate times 38. So fortnightly pay = hourly rate × 38 × 2. For example, at the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour, weekly pay is $1,004.90 and fortnightly pay is $2,009.80. If you work casual hours with 25% loading, your casual hourly rate is $33.05, giving a fortnightly pay of $2,511.80 (before tax and super). Remember that super is paid on top of your ordinary earnings, not deducted from your pay.

faqs.q: What is casual loading and how does it affect my annual conversion?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an extra 25% paid on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for lack of paid leave entitlements. It is set by the Fair Work Commission for award-covered employees. When converting to annual pay, if you are a casual employee, you should use the loaded rate (base × 1.25) in the formula: annual gross = loaded hourly rate × hours per week × 52. For example, the National Minimum Wage casual rate is $33.05 per hour. Assuming 38 hours per week, annual gross is $33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,306.80. Super is then calculated on the ordinary earnings component (the base rate, not the loading), but many employers pay super on the total. Check your award or agreement. The calculator on this site has a checkbox to add 25% casual loading to the base rate you enter – do not enter a rate that already includes loading.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the Annual Pay Conversion

When you have an hourly rate or a salary offer, the first step is to convert it into an annual figure. The standard formula used across Australia is:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**

This assumes you work the same number of hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, allowances, or salary sacrifice. For full-time employees, the typical week is 38 hours, as defined by the Fair Work Ombudsman. If your hours differ, adjust accordingly. The calculator on [the timesheet](/) uses 38 hours as the default, but you can change it.

### Why 38 Hours and 52 Weeks?

The 38-hour week is the standard ordinary hours for full-time employment under most awards and the National Employment Standards. The 52-week year is a simple multiplication – it does not account for unpaid leave or public holidays. For a more precise estimate, you could use 52 weeks minus your annual leave and public holidays, but the formula here provides a consistent baseline.

### Fortnightly Pay

Many Australians are paid fortnightly. To find your fortnightly gross pay, multiply your weekly pay by two. For example, if your hourly rate is $30, weekly pay is $1,140 (30 × 38), and fortnightly pay is $2,280. This is useful for budgeting and comparing with salary offers that are quoted per fortnight.

## Minimum Wage and Award Rates

The **National Minimum Wage** from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for a 38-hour week. Casual employees receive an additional 25% loading, making the casual rate $33.05 per hour. These rates are set by the Fair Work Commission and apply to employees not covered by an award or registered agreement.

Most employees are covered by an award that specifies higher minimum rates for their industry or occupation. You can find your award rate on the Fair Work Ombudsman's [pay guides](/blog). Award rates often include classifications based on skill level and experience. The figures on this site are averages or minimums – they are not a median for your specific job. For example, the Australian Bureau of Statistics' Average Weekly Earnings (May 2026) for full-time adult ordinary time is $2,083.70 per week, which is an average across all industries, not a median for any particular role.

## Casual Loading

If you are a casual employee, your hourly rate includes a 25% loading to compensate for not receiving paid sick leave or annual leave. When converting to annual pay, use the loaded rate. The calculator on [the timesheet](/) has a checkbox that adds 25% to the base rate you enter. **Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading** – let the calculator do the addition.

## Superannuation

Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings, not deducted from your pay. The super guarantee rate is 12% from 1 July 2026, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. For example, if your annual ordinary earnings are $80,000, your employer must contribute $9,600 to your super fund. This is not included in your take-home pay but is a valuable part of your total remuneration.

## Tax and Medicare

Income tax for 2026–27 uses the resident tax-free threshold: no tax on the first $18,200, then 15% on income between $18,201 and $45,000, 30% on $45,001 to $135,000, 37% on $135,001 to $190,000, and 45% above $190,000. The Medicare levy is generally 2% of your taxable income. The calculator on this site uses these rates but does not deduct HELP repayments, the Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging.

## Salary Sacrifice Electric Car

One way to reduce your taxable income is through salary sacrifice, particularly for an electric car. Under current Australian Taxation Office rules, eligible electric cars are exempt from fringe benefits tax, making this a popular option. When you salary sacrifice an electric car, the lease payments and running costs are taken from your pre-tax salary, lowering your taxable income. For example, if your annual gross is $90,000 and you sacrifice $12,000 for an electric car, your taxable income becomes $78,000. This can move you into a lower tax bracket and save you thousands in tax.

However, the annual pay formula on this site does not account for salary sacrifice. You need to manually subtract the annual sacrifice amount from your gross pay to estimate your taxable income. Super is still calculated on your ordinary earnings (the amount before the sacrifice), so your employer's super contributions remain based on the original gross figure.

For more details on how salary packaging interacts with super and tax, see our page on [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging).

## Putting It All Together

Let's walk through an example. Suppose you are a full-time employee earning $35 per hour, working 38 hours per week. Your annual gross is $35 × 38 × 52 = $69,160. Your fortnightly gross is $35 × 38 × 2 = $2,660. Super at 12% adds $8,299.20 on top. Tax on $69,160 is calculated as: $0 on first $18,200, 15% on $26,800 ($18,201 to $45,000) = $4,020, and 30% on $24,160 ($45,001 to $69,160) = $7,248. Total tax = $11,268. Medicare levy at 2% = $1,383.20. Estimated take-home pay = $69,160 - $11,268 - $1,383.20 = $56,508.80 per year, or about $4,709 per month.

If you salary sacrifice an electric car for $10,000 per year, your taxable income drops to $59,160. Tax becomes: $0 + $4,020 + 30% on $14,160 ($45,001 to $59,160) = $4,248. Total tax = $8,268. Medicare = $1,183.20. Take-home = $59,160 - $8,268 - $1,183.20 = $49,708.80, plus you have the car. Your super remains based on $69,160.

## Important Disclaimer

Annual pay here is hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax is the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.

For more reference tables and data, visit our [reference tables](/data) page.
